idiom_name: trait Pricing + Box<dyn Pricing> stored by the context
implementation_notes: A trait is the strategy interface and a trait object is the strategy: Box<dyn Pricing> (owned), &'a dyn Pricing (borrowed) or &'static dyn Pricing (no allocation) stores whichever implementation is selected at run time. The Rust Book's trait-object chapter describes exactly this shape and its cost: a fat pointer carrying the data plus a vtable, a lookup per call, and blocked inlining - the price paid for letting the concrete type be decided after the program starts, or for holding a heterogeneous collection of strategies in one field. Prefer the generic/closure form (second variant) when the choice is fixed at the call site, and note that object safety rules apply: a generic method or one returning Self keeps a trait out of a vtable.
pitfalls: The pointer form is part of the design: Box owns the strategy, &'a dyn borrows it (the context then carries a lifetime), and &'static dyn needs no allocation - choosing late forces every holder of the context to change.
dyn Trait erases the concrete type: downcasting requires Any, and a strategy that must be cloned needs an explicit clone_box method because Clone is not dyn-compatible.
Object safety is a compiler constraint, not a run-time check: a generic method or a method returning Self silently rules the trait out as a trait object, and the error appears at the use site.

variants.name: Generic bound or closure (monomorphised static dispatch, zero cost)
variants.idiom_name: impl Fn / generic parameter S: Strategy (monomorphisation)
variants.implementation_notes: When the strategy is fixed at the call site, take it as a closure (impl Fn, FnMut or FnOnce - which is sugar for a generic parameter) or as a generic type parameter bound by the trait; monomorphisation generates one specialised copy per concrete strategy, so there is no vtable, no allocation and the call inlines. Effective Rust's generics-versus-trait-objects item weighs exactly this trade and names the price: more code, longer compiles and the type parameter spreading into every holder, against a faster call and a single-instance function for the dynamic form. Choose it when the algorithm is known at compile time or varies per call site, and keep the trait when strategies with several operations or state must be named.
pitfalls: Every instantiation produces its own copy of the generic code, so binary size and compile time grow with the number of concrete strategies, and the type parameter leaks into every type that stores the context.

A closure type is unnameable: storing the strategy in a struct requires a generic parameter (or impl Trait in return position), and a closure cannot be used where a dyn Trait is required without boxing it.
Argument-position impl Trait cannot be turbofished, so a caller that must name the strategy type explicitly has to use the full generic bound instead.
